p: Thank you all. Just so I’m clear, so labor and policy standards is getting 27 positions and general counsel is getting 25 positions, is that right?
I believe it’s 29 for labor and policy and–
[interposing] and 20 for general counsel.
Okay. 20 for general counsel?
20 for general– do you want me to go through the division breakdown?
Yeah, and what jobs are they? You know, are they lawyers, paralegals, investigators, researchers?
Sure. So, it’s 20 for GC, I think lawyers–
[interposing] Only lawyers?
No, it’s lawyers and investigators in the– it’s lawyers and investigators in the first fiscal year, and out fiscal years there’ll be additional clerical support staff added.
So, how many lawyers? How many investigators?
The current plan is of those 20, 17 lawyers at different levels of seniority.
17 lawyers, some supervisors I assume in that mix, and then three investigators?
Yes.
And you think that’s the appropriate mix?
Yeah, I think based on– I think this really gives us a chance to thrive as we move forward.

What we’re seeing, Council Member, unsurprising is as we take on bigger firms like Extra Space, a publicly-traded firm, these are serious companies with serious lawyers, and we need to be sure that in settlement negotiations that they don’t go, well, we could take them to court. For that we simply need–
[interposing] You got to lawyer up.
We got to lawyer up.
Okay. Okay, so that’s good. And then you have– you don’t have your projections, because you just want to see how the staffing goes?
I’m sorry, can you say that again?
So, you don’t– because you have 20 for this year, but you don’t have projections what you’re going to do next year?
I mean, I think we do have a sense. I don’t– I’m a little hesitant because obviously as the year progresses, there may be decision made to–
[interposing] You may shift some staffing.
May shift things around. So, I think we do have a general sense. I don’t think that’s necessarily ready for discussion, because I don’t want to like–
[interposing] Yeah, I appreciate that.
[inaudible] right now.
Okay. And then Office of Labor Policy and Standards, you said– what’s 29, 10 investigators we said.
Right. So I’ve written down since you asked me the questions.
Yay.
So, we’ve got 11 lawyers, 10 investigators and e-data scientists, and that includes the supervisory staff in each category.

Great. And you think both in both sections of the Department that is going to get you in a sufficient place to deal with any backlog and all these future, you know, issues that are coming forward? You know, we have 10,000 potential Uber/Lyft deactivations coming down the pike. We’re having 2,000 new potential street vendor licenses, not to mention laundry workers, not to mention security guards, not to mention every other thing that we’re going to do, you know. Council Member Caban talked about Last Mile. you know, there’s like things that are coming– that might be coming forward. I want to be clear that do you think there will not be a backlog when consumers and workers are coming to your office, we’re not going to tell them wait six months now when we’re staffed up.

That’s our projection at this point, Chair. You know, I’ll say those numbers we just rattled off of course for FY 27, there are additional confusions for all of my

colleagues here in FY28 and then further in FY29, but again, we’re going to– this isn’t going to be– we’re going to be continuously evaluated in this. If delivery protection passes, I hope it does, we’re going to have additional needs for lines. We’re going to be monitoring the student loan market place. We might need additional OTPS outreach there. So, we’re going to be monitoring this. We could see a big spike, an unexpected spike. You know, we’ve already seen an increase in worker complaints in 2026. That is going to make it harder to close the backlog, but again, we have accounted for that in this budget. But we have to be monitoring our complaints as we will be, and we have to be monitoring our backlog as we are, and of course monitoring the new laws that are coming online.

And can you just update us? You know, I mean, obviously I’m pushing to give you more money, so here you go. But I would just be concerned that we get past the budget and then we see in the summer or in the fall that you’ve hired up and there still is a backlog, you know, where– you know, in January there’s a backlog because you’ve hired up and you trained people. So, I’m just

concerned. Can we get ongoing updates about where staffing is, making sure that if there is that six-month backlog or it’s been reduced to three months, or?

Certainly. Certainly. And the goal again is to see that backlog fall. And again, it’s a little bit like going uphill because the complaints are rising. So we need to hire faster than the complaints are rising and deal with the backlog. And with respect to certain laws like deactivation, as you mentioned, there’s going to be a lookback period. So the thousands of workers who are deactivated over the last six years– six years you’re going to be able to have those six or five, seven– seven years going to be able to have those deactivations revisited. So, we made the best projection we could based on the numbers we see now, and you know, that’s going to change to some degree in a couple months, and we’re happy to keep updated on it.
I’d appreciate that.

Yes, Chair, just to echo the Commissioner, we’re happy to provide you updates there, and then also we have other periods in

the budgetary cycle like the November Plan where we can always come back and discuss more with OMB our new needs.

Thank you. And so grocery store delivery services like Instacart, you know, you gave– granted temporary exemption for minimum wage payments through July 2026. Are you guys prepared to ensure full compliance with that in July?
Yes, we are, and it’s my expectation that the delivery apps will be as well.

Yes, absolutely. So, we are getting reports from Instacart. We’re already monitoring their wage payments, their work time, trip time, and on-call time, and just for the record, you know, no full exception, right? They are required to pay the full minimum pay rate for all trip time and will be required soon to pay for all on-call time as well.
And what kind of staffing you think that’s going to require on your behalf?

I mean, luckily on this– in this area, you know, it is already part of laws that we’re enforcing in the minimum pay rate. So we already have structures in place to analyze the reports that we get from apps, and so that fits in neatly with work that we’re already doing to monitor Uber, to monitor DoorDash, and we are already doing that with Instacart, too.
So, you don’t expect a flood over the summer of new complaints?

You never know when you’re going to get a flood, you know? I mean, an app can change a certain procedure in a way that confuses workers, whether or not it's legal, but you know, one of the benefits of the structure of these laws is that we’re able to watch and get the data reporting from the apps on a monthly basis so that we’re not only relying on complaints from workers, but also able to watch and identify issues through those reports.

So, you know, with the new street vendor licenses there’s going to be some penalties associated with that, and I know mostly DSNY is going to be doing enforcement. And

what role do you think you’re going to play in coordination with DSNY on that level of enforcement, and what role do you think you’ll play in the new licensing scheme on the enforcement side?

Our real role is to stand side by side with the street vendors and help them, help bring them out of the shadows into the New York economy with licenses. So, certainly I can see a role for us educating people along with SVP, along with Council Members who I know are interested in this, but in terms of day-to-day enforcement, for example the sanitation code, we’re going to leave that to DSNY and Health.

Yeah. I mean, I’m worried about people not knowing, right? So, I’m worried about your role and ensuring that the small businesses understand to avoid the enforcement. You know, nothing to speak against my district or some people in my community. I can see someone not liking a new vendor on street corner and calling every day, and I want to make sure those vendors don’t get to a place where they could have enforcement issues.

Well, if someone doesn’t have a license, that would be our

responsibility. But again, our goal, the reason our administration reversed the last administration to endorse this bill is we want people to get licenses. We want small businesses to thrive. So, you know, again, we have a statutory responsibility to make sure folks are licensed, but at the end of the day, the orientation of our agency is squarely on the side of the street vendors who the council decided and we agreed it’s long overdue they get the licenses.

And Chair, I would mention as well, I think a lot of the resources that you’re talking about, you know, the vision of street vendor services at SBS is actually– they’re revamping their website to include a lot of education material. That has included feedback from individual agencies like the DCWP, DOHMH, and DSNY to ensure that vendors understand kind of the rules of the road, including mapping that’s out there, as well as plain language descriptions of their restrictions on the street.

You know, I mentioned this earlier, I’ll just flag again this kind of outreach it’ll be critical to avoid these common enforcement issues, and I– you know, I would love to see the administration commit to some of

those resources to these organizations who are going to help prevent people from getting these fine and fees and be affected by enforcement.
Absolutely, and I’m happy to go with you in our district to some of our local street vendors to get the word out.
Great. We’ll schedule that. I’m happy to do it.
Chair, certainly heard on this issue you’re raising about funding, so we’ll make sure to raise that with our colleagues at OMB and City Hall.

Yeah. So, I just want to go back to junk fees. What are you seeing now on junk fees based on the Executive Order? Where are you seeing violations? Kind of, how are those moving forward? Are you seeing a spike since the enactment?
We’re paying more attention to it, I think is how–
[interposing] Okay.

Let me put it this way, I think in the past, you know, we looked at different categories, employment agencies,

immigration services providers, etcetera, etcetera. Now we’re sort of creating a new category the way we’re thinking about it. Who are charging unlawful fees? So, we did a warning blitz with employment agencies. We did a warning blitz with used car dealers. We did a warning blitz with immigration service providers. We did the warning blitz and the rule with hotels. And I can tell you now, you know, we also co-chair the Junk Fee Taskforce. We just held a meeting yesterday on this with other agencies, and I don’t want to get ahead of the mayor or other agencies, but I can tell you other agencies are doing a really thoughtful job of identifying junk fees that frankly we wouldn’t necessarily have visibility into, but because say department– well, name any departments– that our sister agencies have deep visibility into and understanding of their authorities. So I’m very optimistic about the trajectory on this. We’re working very hard both on enforcement and rule-making. I think Mike wants to add some more.

Yeah, just some additional color to add to that, Chair and Council Members. As the Commissioner alluded to, this has

been sort of not always labeled as a junk fee, but core to our work over the last several years. We’ve brought three cases recently at OATH over the last 18 months against licensed employment agencies for charging illegal advance fees. What are those? Those are just junk fees by another name. Similarly, we have great laws passed by this council, supplemented by our rules, on financing disclosures and what can be charged by used car dealerships. We call them second-hand automobile dealers. And we are constantly bringing cases where that’s a core part of the investigation. We actually have a major trial ongoing right now at the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings against a major dealership, Victory Mitsubishi. We of course pass the– as the Commissioner alluded to– the hotel junk fee rule. We’re monitoring the complaints. I’m always talking about the consumer complaints. Please give us complaints. We’re monitoring complaints. We’re filing our first summons under that rule imminently. So, this is something that we’re always looking at, we’ve always looked at traditionally, and this has been very helpful to name this exact sort of concept and to really like focus our work. And let me just

underscore, the Executive Order is very helpful in doing that, and also looking forward to the different types of junk fees and pricing violations that may not exist. This really transcends just narrow junk fees, but sort of the ideas that we’ve been talking about, about surveillance pricing, dynamic pricing, sort of the new generation of how consumers are harmed on a day-to-day basis. And so we have our–
[interposing] You’re getting in front of our hearing in a couple weeks.

I’m sorry. You got me going, and I just– it’s like our ear to the ground on that. So we’re looking for trends and sort of this commitment by the admin is this type of issue, junk fees, pricing. These are things that we are going to dedicate resources to now in a way that’s really going to result in dividends for New Yorkers.

Yeah. I appreciate that, and hopefully you’ll have the resources you need to be doing that work. So, summer– it’s sounds like you’ve moved forward with not extending their contract to do student loan work in our city for general New Yorkers.
For city residents. We’re continuing the program for city employees.

And then who’s picking up that support to ensure the city residents who have student loans? Anyone on the dais, anyone’s got student loans– how are people going to be able to access the services? What kind of outreach you're doing in communities to make sure people are aware of this issue?

This is a very high priority for us, and I think we’ve been– I’ve been having conversations with our folks every day or almost every day on this for weeks now, especially our financial empowerment folks. Number of points– first, we– our financial empowerment centers not only provide– our counselors are not only trained on student loans. They’re trained on credit card debt, auto debt, all manners of debt. One push we’re really going to make this summer, so to speak, is pushing more New Yorkers into our financial empowerment centers. We do have capacity there. And again, we can provide– those are one-on-one personalized in-person services, and they could provide really– our financial empowerment centers can

take a holistic look at New Yorkers’ financial health, not just student loans, but credit card, medical debt, etcetera to put people on a firmer path forward. We’re also working this summer to make sure there’s no abrupt disruption to people’s accounts. We want to make sure that people continue to be served into the summer and that then we can transition them into vital services. But the fact of the matter is, and this is why I think Intro 177 was so critical, we are facing a huge cliff in New York City with the Trump administration’s, I think, reckless treatment of– and callous treatment of student loan borrowers. It is critical that we double our efforts to get the word out around resources that the city is available. That is something our outreach team is working very hard on. It’s also critical we work with partners in the state. I’ve talked to you in the past about working with DFS. That is something that we are planning to do. Stay tuned on that. About making sure we’re reaching the most– the people most likely to face default. We’re also– we’ve had meetings with EDCAP [sic]. The state I think in a very wise move significantly expanded funding for EDCAP to expand those services. EDCAP to

us is not a rival at all. It is a complement. I really think this requires an all-hands-on-deck response by the city and the state, because the federal government isn’t here to help. It’s here to make people’s lives worse.

I appreciate hearing that. I know we’ve talked about this before, and we’d love to partner in doing those kind of outreach events whether they go to financial empowerment centers– some of our offices just getting the word out.
Yeah.
And I hope that we can start doing that in the next few weeks.
Absolutely. I think we’ve had conversations already about that.

And the last thing I want to talk about is docketing and wondering kind of– are you– how many cases are you docketing, judgements for workers? What does that look like? Is that being successful or not? Are people getting their money back? Like is the docketing power and authority working for the agency?
Carlos stole my table of contents, so it’s taking me a minute. Do you want to jump in on there, Liz?

Sure. Thankfully, it’s a power we very rarely need to use. We have a very, very high rate of collection in the Office of Labor Policy and Standards on our worker protection cases. We– this is in part because we settle virtual– almost all of our cases settle, and they settle with very strong terms to ensure that companies actually pay. We require companies to sign a Confession of Judgement in almost all of our settlements, and always when there’s a payment plan. And so that ensures we’re able to obtain the money for workers.
Do you have any cases where you’ve had to docket judgements?
We have, and have had some success in actually collecting them. I’m hesitating only because some even come from before that law went into effect.

Yeah, I mean, I think– I think this is an important tool. Thank you for in your prior role sort of leading the charge to

get us docketing authority, and I think that it hasn’t come up all that often, but it is valuable when it has happened.
Alright, right. Well, I want to thank you, and Chair, I’m finished my questions. Thank you.

Okay. And with that, I think we are done with this portion of this hearing. So, thank you so much, Commissioner and to everyone on your team, and we’re just going to take a couple minutes to transition over to EDC. Thank you.
Thank you, Chairs.
Thank you very much.
Thank you to the Council. [break]

Okay. Good afternoon everyone, and welcome to the third FY27 Executive Budget hearing for the day focusing on New York City Economic Development corporation. I’m Council Member Linda Lee and I’m pleased to be joined by our Speaker, Julie Menin, as well as Chair Virginia Maloney, Chair of the Committee on Economic

Development. And we have been joined today by our Deputy Speaker, Council Member Brewer, Council Member Thomas-Henry, and I think that’s it for now. Okay. So, welcome to our interim President and CEO Jeanny Pak and to your team, and I just have to say this from the record, a sister from another mister. As a fellow Korean, it’s very– we don’t see this often where there’s Korean-American women especially who are in positions like this. So, very happy to see you in this role. So, I just wanted to say that.
Thank you so much. Likewise.

Thank you all for joining us today to answer our questions. And on May 12th, 2026 the administration released the Executive Financial Plan for fiscal 26 to 2030 with a proposed FY27 budget of $124.7 billion. The Economic Development Corporation’s proposed FY27 budget of $60.5 million represents less than 0.1 percent of the administration’s proposed FY27 budget the Executive Plan. Although EDC manages a large portfolio of assets on behalf of the city which generate revenue not capture in the funding pass-through, the Department of Small Business Services. And this is

an increase of $29.9 million or 97.9 percent from the $30.6 million originally budgeted in the FY27 Preliminary Plan. This increase results from several actions, but is driven primarily by the addition of $20 million for the city-backed insurance program and the rollover of $7.1 million for the Cannabis Impact Fund. As one of the primary drivers of economic growth in our city, now is a critical time for EDC to ensure that we are maximizing return from programs that generate tax revenue so that we are able to provide the many critical services that our agencies undertake and that we are developing initiatives to help address the affordability crisis New Yorkers are facing. I commend the administration on the inclusion of the city-backed insurance program, as we have long heard from affordable housing developers and advocates about the barrier that rising insurance costs have created on developing more and maintaining existing affordable housing developments. We are excited to hear more about the vision of this program and how the funding included in this plan will play into the mayor’s broader housing plan. And now I want to turn it over to Speaker Menin for her opening remarks.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee, and I want to thank Chair Lee and Chair Maloney for conducting this important hearing. Good morning to interim President and CEO Pak, and I want to thank you and the rest of the EDC staff for being here this afternoon. The EDC is a key player in fostering economic growth, developing workforces and improving the sustainability of our city holds a vital role in ensuring that these many benefits are spread equitably across all of our communities. I do want to say at the outset that I have– and I’ve been speaking about this for several months– am concerned about the job loss that’s happening in our city. The fact that we have lost about 27,000 jobs compared to the job growth that we have seen each and every year in the prior four years, and I think this is something that has to be addressed, and it’s something that we are deeply concerned about. Today, I want to explore some of the key allocations that are included in EDC’s fiscal 2027 Executive Budget and Capital Commitment Plan. As you know, the administration has also included $70 million for the program to create a system of publicly funded grocery stores. I do want to be clear that the Council absolutely agrees that

grocery prices are too expensive, and we must lower the price of groceries. That’s one of the many reasons why we have introduced bills to ban dynamic pricing around grocery prices as well as surveillance pricing. So that’s something that we are very committed to. Today, we want to hear from the administration about how the impacts of this specific proposal would impact bodegas and other small grocery stores that are in close proximity to the planned new stores. So, we want to understand that impact from EDC as well as the impact on workers at those businesses so we can better understand and ensure that bodegas, grocery stores, and workers at those stores are not adversely impacted. In addition, I’m looking forward to learning about how the addition of $100 million over the next three fiscal years for the city backed insurance program will help to reduce property and liability insurance premiums which is something that we have been very focused on at the council on the insurance angle and our new Insurance Accountability Office. So, we want to understand the impact on affordable and rent stabilized housing, and so we’re looking forward to hearing your testimony in that regard. So, once again, I want to thank the

Chairs for their leadership and the EDC team for being here, and we look forward to a very productive hearing. So, let me pass it back to our Finance Chair.
Great. Thank you. And I will pass it to Chair Maloney.

Thank you. I’m honored to Chair the Committee– Council’s Committee on Economic Development and to be joined by our Finance Chair Lee as well as Speaker Menin for this important conversation. We’re going to be hearing today from the Interim President of NYC EDC on the fiscal 2027 Executive Budget, including the Executive Capital Commitment Plan. As we move towards budget adoption, it’s important that EDC’s investments reflect its core priorities of growing innovation sectors, delivering sustainable communities, and strengthen this city’s future economy. This committee looks forward to discussing how the Executive Budget is going to advance those goals and how the investments will translate into tangible benefits for New Yorkers. The largest investment included in this plan is for the city backed insurance program supported by $20 million in fiscal

year 2027, increasing to $40 million in 2028 and 2029, totalling $100 million over three years. For too long affordable housing developers and providers have been constricted by rising insurance costs with insurance premiums having more than doubled since 2017. So, this investment targets one of the highest operating costs for developers and comes at a critical time. We look forward to hearing more details about the program, how it will be structured to drive premiums down. The Executive Capital Commitment Plan covers fiscals 2026 to 2030 and includes $3.5 billion for EDC. That’s a 16.8 percent decrease from the fiscal year 2027 Preliminary Capital Commitment Plan we discussed in March. That plan has a 10-year commitment and includes $7.1 billion. Only a small increase of $4.8 million from the Preliminary Plan. So, this change reflects a stretching of funds that were originally allocated within the next five years out to the 10-year plan, and we’re interested in hearing why these timelines have changed, whether any critical projects that EDC funds like Hunts Point Produce Market or Inwood Greenway will be impacted by those changes. And third, the plan includes the $30 million allocated

for city backed grocery stores. Since our first hearing, two of the five sites have now been identified, and we’d like a lot more detail on how these stores will operate, the criteria for site selection, the timeline for getting these up and running, and how they will balance minimizing taxpayer subsidy while delivering on the promise of making essential household groceries more affordable. I want to thank the Interim President Jeanny Pak for being here, as well as the Chief of Staff, Jenn Montalvo, as well as the rest of EDC staff for coming here and testifying, and I want to thank everyone’s who’s been incredibly responsive to our many requests. We would not have been able to analyze the city’s budget at such a detailed level without EDC’s partnership. So, I commend your leadership in this interim period. And I also want to thank the Finance Staff, Spencer Coon [sp?], Hector German [sp?], Daniel Krupp [sp?], Emry Edev [sp?], Chima Obicheri [sp?] for their work preparing for this hearing, and the committee staff, Alex Polonof [sp?], William Hungyang for their support, as well as my own staff that put in a lot of effort, Sophie Secor [sp?], Isabella Saldono [sp?], Anne Kaveri Kutageri [sp?]

for all their hard work to prepare. And I’ll now defer back to the Finance Chair.

Thank you. And before we begin the testimony, just wanted to remind everyone that for this year’s budget hearings we’re doing all the public testimony on the same day on Wednesday, June 10th, beginning at 9:30. So, please make sure to sign up for the public testimony portion which again is Wednesday, June 10th beginning at 9:30. And I will now turn it over to Brian Sarfo, our Committee Counsel, who I would also love to thank for all of his hard work sitting here and keeping me in check. Okay. Take it away.

Good afternoon. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Commissioner Pak? And oh– you may begin.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Speaker Menin, Chair Lee, Chair Maloney, and members of the Economic Development and Finance Committees. Well, we are back here again and I’m still here. My name is Jeanny Pak and I continue to serve as the Interim President and CEO of New York

City Economic Development Corporation as well as the Chief Financial Officer. I am here with my Chief of Staff, Jennifer Montalvo, and I’d just like to begin to say in the two months since I last testified before you at the Preliminary Budget hearing, EDC has continued advancing our work to make our city more affordable and livable. Together with the Mayor and Deputy Mayor Julie Su, EDC is reimagining economic development with a focus on economic growth that both expands economic pie for all New Yorkers and ensure the pie includes and elevates working people who have previously and historically been left behind. Before I jump into our projects, I want to zoom out quickly and give a sense of where our economy is. Despite continued national and international headwinds, New York City’s economy remains resilient. Labor force participation is at an all-time high. Real estate and citywide vacancies continues to improve. Venture capital investment in our city reached its strongest quarter in five years, and the city continues to attract more college graduates with one in four New Yorkers or 2.1 million residents who live in New York City between the ages of 18 and 34. Yet, we know we are continuing to face real challenges as well as the

increasing pressure of affordability. We know that far too many New Yorkers feel the city they love is becoming more and more unaffordable. For this reason, EDC takes a forward-looking approach to economic growth and development. We will continue to use every tool in our toolbox to build a more economically just New York City. Today, I’ll use my time to share a handful of updates on work that has seen significant progress since March. These initiatives are advancing mayoral priorities on affordability and represent major wins for the city and working people. Public groceries: Mayor Mamdani has been clear, the working people of this city should be able to afford the basic needs and services this city has to offer, and that includes healthy food and groceries. Today, as the result of rising cost of rent, gas, bills, and food, more and more New Yorkers can’t afford everyday healthy groceries. Making sure working people can buy fresh affordable groceries is a key part of the mayor’s affordability agenda. In March, I shared that EDCwas working closely with the administration on the public groceries initiative to increase food access to fresh healthy food at a price New Yorkers can afford. That work has continued and intensified and

has led to two major announcements to date with concrete milestones toward realizing this vision. In April, I stood with the mayor in East Harlem as he announced La Marqueta as the first site for NYC Groceries. As one of the city’s six public markets operated by EDC, La Marqueta supports more than 20 small businesses and 120 workers, including restaurants, art vendors, and community organizations. Now, as a future Manhattan site for NYC Groceries, La Marqueta will further benefit the East Harlem community by offering affordable food to working-class New Yorkers. The 9,000 square foot store will be constructed from the ground up with a significant community outreach and input to ensure it reflects the diverse cultures of El Barrio and is expected to open in 2029. And just last Monday, I joined the mayor again, this time in Hunts Point in the Bronx to announce the second NYC grocery store. This one will be at the Peninsula, the redeveloped site of the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Center. EDC is leading the transformation of the site into a campus of dignified living, a place where Bronxites can afford to live, work, and play. The peninsula development includes 740 units of 100

percent affordable housing, a childcare center, 30,000 square feet for commercial light industrial businesses providing good paying jobs, and over 50,000 square feet for community, cultural, and recreational open space. With this new NYC grocery store, they will now have access to healthy affordable food right in their backyard. This 20,000 square foot store will be the first NYC Groceries site to open, expected by the end of 2027. Along with the peninsula, the mayor also announced an online portal for private property owners to recommend sites for future NYC grocery stores in Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island. The portal created by EDC will support early identification and screening of potential sites and inform next steps and timeline for three other NYC Groceries locations. I’m incredibly proud of EDC’s work on NYC Groceries initiative. This is what public investment should look like, making sure that benefits and the prosperity of our city reach working people who need it most. Beyond our long-term stewardship and advancement of the sites where these two stores will be located, our team has been working tirelessly to develop this initiative and ensure that the basic

needs of working people and families are met. Public restrooms: In March I shared that EDC has released the RFP for modular restrooms across the city to expand access to public bathrooms, one of the mayor’s first 100 days commitments. This $4 million pilot program will make sure that more New Yorkers will have more access to public bathrooms. Bathrooms are basic public infrastructure and access to them should be easier. We anticipate an update on the RFP soon. Housing: EDC views housing production as an essential economic infrastructure. Affordable housing enables workers and New Yorkers to live near jobs, to raise their families, build roots in the community. It supports economic mobility and underpins the neighborhood vitality across the five boroughs, but today New York City is facing an existential affordability and housing crisis. As the Mayor has said, New York cannot remain a city of opportunity if the people who make this city run are priced out of it. At EDC we’re advancing affordable housing development across the city and that includes going after the structural costs that are driving up the price of housing. Insurance is one of them with the price of insurance tripling since 2017. This April

we announced the first city-backed insurance program to help New Yorkers stay in their homes, give building owners the support they need to make repairs, and building affordable housing more affordable. The insurance program will reduce the cost of property and liability insurance for affordable and rent stabilized housing. EDC is partnering with HDC and HPD to develop and execute the insurance program which aims to issue new insurance policies for 20,000 units of housing next year, and 100,000 homes by 2030. Additionally, the city expects a five to seven times return measured in city capital subsidy savings. Lower insurance costs help to increase property level income which supports larger property level loans and reduces the subsidy capital required in new construction and preservation deals. This program uses the city’s purchasing power to lower insurance premiums for affordable housing and rent stabilized apartments, helping our investments reach more New Yorkers and is a key part of the city’s housing plan. World Cup: Finally, in just 13 days our city will welcome the world for the 2016 FIFA World Cup. As I am sure you have all seen, the mayor has been making a number of announcements

to activate our city during the 39-day tournament, ensuring working people, New Yorkers, and tourists alike enjoy all that the five boroughs have to offer, and EDC continues to play a big role from free fan fests, watch parties, and fan zones at our public markets on our biggest campuses, including the already-announced Staten Island University Hospital Community Park, and more locations to be announced very soon, to the Dress the City Campaign that will show off host city’s soccer jerseys, inspiring New Yorkers to get into the game. EDC is working tirelessly to ensure the World Cup kicks goals for working people this summer. I know some of you are ferry riders, and I hope you all get the chance to see five wrapped NYC ferries which we unveiled last week, each with a borough-specific wrapping, showcasing the energy, diversity and pride of our city. They will be on our harbor this summer as part of the World Cup festivities. The World Cup is a tremendous opportunity for us to promote New York City as a place to live, visit, and conduct business. As I said in March, this is a rare moment to show a global audience of tourists, companies, investors, and delegations that there’s no better place to do

business than New York City. As I mentioned, these are just a couple of EDC’s most notable highlights. Across all of our work, we are proud of our partnership with the City Council to improve the lives of our neighbors, increase affordability, expand opportunity, and ensure New York City remains a global hub of business, culture, and innovation. I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today, and we welcome any questions you have.

Thank you. Really quickly want to recognize we’ve been joined by Council Members Riley, Council Member Morano on Zoom, Council Member Farías, and Council Member Epstein. And Speaker Menin, go ahead with your questions.

Thank you. Okay, thank you very much for the testimony. I mean, I really want to start with something that I referred to in my opening statement which is I’m deeply concerned about the job loss in New York City from the past year, and in this testimony I didn’t hear anything about job creation at all. What is EDC’s plan to focus on job creation and job retention? So, it’s not only about creating new jobs, it’s also making sure that we’re retaining the jobs that currently exist in the city.

Yeah, thanks for that question. You know, we understand the headwinds that’s happening nationally and globally and New York City is affected as all the other major cities in the United States. But we do know that New York City is resilient, and from 9/11 to the financial crisis to coming out of COVID, it has proven to be an incredibly resilient city primarily because, you know, this is New York City and we have the best talent in the world and the greatest infrastructure. So, we are comforted by a few statistics that I’ll share with you. We have an economic group that puts out a monthly snapshot. It came out today, so hopefully you’ll be able to see it. But a couple of things are– labor participation is at an all-time high. Our commercial leases have had the highest two consecutive quarters since 2019. VC [sic] investments are the highest since 2021. Our unemployment rate is fairly low at 5.6 percent, although BIPOC is higher at 7.3. So that’s something that we are committed to looking at and addressing. And tourism, transit ridership, all are doing well, and why is that? I mean, we have the top talent of– top destination for talent. We have over a million of college student

and recent college graduates which are an incredible pull. Year over year, New York City actually has increased jobs by 28,000, and 5,000 since– in 2026 year-to-date. So, this is more than other comparable metros such as Miami, D.C., Boston that actually have had decreased jobs, and New York City has increased jobs. This is on par with like Dallas. So, we’re not doing worse than Dallas. We’re doing about similar to Dallas, but we’re doing a lot better in terms of jobs from our comparable cities. And you know, what is EDC doing? We believe New York City is an innovation economy. We have a dedicated business development group that works closely with business generators, that people are interested in coming, as well as businesses that are thinking of growing here in New York City. we want to retain. Like you said, we want to retain companies. So, Amex committing to 10,000 jobs in the World Trade Center, Anthropic doubling their size. These are all great commitments and it’s proof New York City is a great place to thrive.

Okay. I just have a couple of responses on that, because you referred to 9/11, and certainly after 9/11– and I served for many

years on the Board of the Lower Manhattan Redevelopment Corporation. We launched specific programs to retain businesses. I mean, that is why many businesses ended up staying in lower Manhattan and moving to lower Manhattan. My concern is that in particular with what is happening around AI, we’re going to see increased job displacement, and if we do not put in plans in place right now to retain companies here and to also attract new companies, I’m very concerned about that. I’m concerned around media and entertainment, that you have job loss to other states. And we’re seeing in the financial sector where there are now more jobs in the financial sector in the state of Texas than there are in New York. That's truly shocking. We used to have triple the number not that long ago. And so again, I’m just urging EDC to start putting in place those plans to make sure that we are fully prepared to retain these businesses and to attract new businesses. And last thing I will mention is, you know, you talked about tourism. The tourism numbers are not great. We know that Broadway year to year is down. Hotel occupancy year to year is down. So, I just– we see all the warning signs, and it’s incumbent upon us as

government then to put in plans in place to deal with that.

Yeah, we appreciate that. We appreciate your observations there. We are working hard every day. Again, I think– we have a dedicated business development team. We also have an innovations– industry group that focus on– you know, as like, New York City while it’s stable businesses such as finance and tech, it is also an innovations economy. So, we want to make sure that we’re growing, like, the next generation of companies, and we’re doing that especially with Green Economy [sic], Tech AI, Life Science, etcetera. So, we are committed to growing that. And also, I think what is really clear to us that we want to make sure that these are good paying jobs and that they’re accessing people who normally don’t have access to these jobs. Part of that is through a lot of the programs that we have like the finding founder fellowship. We also have a lot of sort of industrial-related construction programs that ensures that other people who small businesses have not been part of these large construction jobs such as Construct NYC. Waterfront Pathways is another program that we have that makes

sure that our maritime work addresses a lot of new companies coming into the industry. Because industries are always and constantly changing. So, we are focused on that. And I guess the other piece of this is affordability piece that part of economic growth is ensuring that the people that live and work here can afford New York City and that they stay here and that they’re not going to leave New York City because it’s too expensive. And so we’re very focused, as you might imagine, on the affordability part of it.

And let me just be clear, we totally agree with that. We are all in on building more affordable housing. On the affordable groceries plan, like to be clear as I said in my testimony, we completely agree that grocery prices are extremely high and that we have to figure out what we can do about that, which is why we’re very focused on funding food pantries. We’re very focused on funding a number of organizations that are currently doing a

lot of work in this space in New York. As I mentioned, we’re focused on banning surveillance pricing, dynamic pricing. Yeah, so–
[interposing] And what will be the impact on them?

New York City– NYC Groceries is focused on, you know,

fresh, healthy foods and everyday groceries to be affordable. We’re not going to– it’s going to be a regular grocery store, but we’re not going to discount everything. So, we’re focused on fresh, healthy foods and everyday groceries. How we selected the sites is we prioritized public sites. That was first and foremost. And so we did an inventory of all the public sites. We also wanted to make sure that from the city’s measure that it was– did not have enough grocery stores per capita. There’s a specific DCP measure. And we also wanted to make sure that it was going to be able to be constructed and online fairly quickly. It isn’t going to take, you know, a decade. So, we were committed to opening all five stores by the end of 2029 with the first one opening by the end of 2027. So, the first site that we announced which will be open by 2029 is La Marqueta. That is a city site, and we’ve been up there. It has a public market there. It has other– sort of it’s like a eight-block site which has all the different uses, and one of it– and it’s being renovated and reimagined, and one of it is an empty lot, and that empty lot was going to be a farmer’s market. So there was going to be city dollars giong

into that to convert it to a farmer’s market, and through our discussions, we realized that this would be a great place for NYC Groceries. So, this peninsula site is– so that’s a ground-up construction so that’s very specific. That’s why it’s not going to be open until 2029. The peninsula, as you know, is the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Center. It’s a development that the EDC and the city’s been working on for some time. It’s going to 704 units of housing. A lot of it’s going to be family housing. It’s in three phases, and we’re pretty much through phase one and about to launch phase two. But phase three, contemplated, which is not going to happen for several years, is– was going to have a grocery store. It was required to have a grocery store. So, there’s a real shortage of grocery stores up there. There’s not really any one– any grocery store close by. So, we decided that we were going to accelerate that grocery store that was going to be online for– constructed in phase three and bring it today, and that’s– and it was also a space that was ready to be tenant– to fit out into a grocery store. It was sort of like poised for kind of a perfect location and structure for a grocery store, and so we selected

that one as a second site that we announced, but it’ll be the first one open by the end of 2027.
But how much are the groceries going to cost?
Well, the grocery– you mean in terms of the discount?
Yeah.

Okay. So, how we’re doing this is that we’re going– in the summer we’re going to put out an RFEI for third-party operator, City Grocery operator, and through that structure they’re going to be operating a grocery store like a normal grocery store, and we’re going to have in that RFEI a core basket of goods that will be discounted. What we’re offering the operator is the city paying the tenant fit-out. This is a substantial cost that the grocery operator would normally have to pay. They are not going to have to pay rent and they’re not going to pay property tax. So, we're going to ensure that that subsidy directly goes to the food affordability of those core baskets, and then we’re going to work out all the details. Once the RFP comes out, you’ll see, you know, some of the details

and then ongoing negotiations with the city operator. It might be one. It might be multiple.
A couple of questions. So, what are the basket of goods that will be covered? What’s included in that?
So, we’re still working that out, but the focus is fresh, healthy foods and every day groceries. So, think bread, milk, meat, chicken, eggs.

[interposing] Produce.

Okay. I know other members have a bunch of questions on that, so I’m going to move topics to city-backed insurance. So, I just want to better understand, because we’re very interested in the issue of insurance and lowering insurance costs. This is incredibly important. Can you explain what the benefit is in having EDC administer the contract, but you’re not managing the program?

This has been a program that have– we've been working with HPD and HDC for actually a few years now, and so we’re really excited that this is now happening and funded. So, the relationship, it’s a three-way effort, and we’re working very closely with HPD and HDC. HPD because they have the housing stock and they are building affordable housing. HDC, because they’re the bond finance arm for the affordable housing. And so it was a really good synergy. So, we’re actually going to be doing this sort of transacting and executing of the insurance program.
And what methodology is being utilized to determine the appropriate funding level for the program?

So, $100 million has been allocated. It’s going to be rolled out and scaled up starting in $20 million and then $40 and $40 in the subsequent years. And so we think that that is going to provide about 20,000 units in the first year and

over 100– about 100,000 by 2030. We are also hoping– again, the city is going to be like an investor, and we’re hoping it might attract other investors and so we can scale that up as time goes on. Okay. And two last questions and I’m going to pass it over to Chair Lee. So, for the program, how is it determined that the program would be able to provide assistance for 20,000 homes by 2027 and 100,000 by 2030?

I can get back to you the actual calculator, but the idea is that, you know, insurance costs have ballooned like 20 to 30 percent over the last few years, and we analyzed it and it’s largely due to overhead and profit and also, you know, EDC in the city has the lowest cost of capital. So, those things combined allow us to offer lower premiums. So, we estimated that it could do 20,000 units and then 100,000. What that will also do is provide savings, so to speak, for the HPD subsidy five to seven times, because you can– because it’s going to be less costly to bring us affordable

housing. To build affordable housing, you’ll need less city subsidy for those HPD sites.
